prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

In Tunis we try to discuss divorce And dying but give up to lounge With rug merchants under a plum tree. From its corner the lamb’s severed head Watches the flies drink from its eyes And its fat disappear into the fire. The light rinses the edge of your sandal, The two wasps that ornament the blur Of screened window. My grandmother Would have loved a night like this. In the wind chimes I can hear her tea cart With its china rolling through Cook Street’s Stony yard one summer when I was always Thirsty, and she moved like a figure On a clock from my lawn chair to the cart, Or swabbed me with alcohol, or cut My hair with the straight razor. I was a week out of the hospital. Beneath my breasts an incision was crossed With stitches of surgical thread. The scalpel came so close it gave My heart a quick kiss. I nearly died. Years later I can still see the skin Flutter on the inside of my left breast And my heart limps like a great uncle Who, because he was a Jew and lame, Was dragged by cossacks across the steppes. He became a friend asking a favor Of a horse who ran so hard, so perfectly Hard, that the green grass rose to meet him.

outputs.L1:
In Tunis, we try to discuss divorce  
and dying, but give up and lounge  
with rug merchants beneath a plum tree.  
From its corner, the lamb’s severed head  
watches the flies drink from its eyes  
as its fat disappears into the fire.  
The light rinses the edge of your sandal,  
the two wasps ornamenting the blur  
of the screened window. My grandmother  
would have loved a night like this.  
In the wind chimes, I can hear her tea cart,  
its china rolling through Cook Street’s  
stony yard one summer when I was always  
thirsty, and she moved like a figure  
on a clock—from my lawn chair to the cart—  
or swabbed me with alcohol, or cut  
my hair with a straight razor.  

I was a week out of the hospital.  
Beneath my breasts, an incision was crossed  
with stitches of surgical thread.  
The scalpel came so close it gave  
my heart a quick kiss. I nearly died.  
Years later, I can still see the skin  
flutter on the inside of my left breast,  
and my heart limps like a great-uncle  
who, because he was a Jew and lame,  
was dragged by Cossacks across the steppes.  
He became a friend asking a favor  
of a horse who ran so hard, so perfectly  
hard, that the green grass rose to meet him.
outputs.L2:
In Tunis, we begin conversations about death and the end of marriage, but abandon them to rest beneath a plum tree among carpet sellers. Nearby, a decapitated lamb’s head lies watching as flies draw moisture from its eyes and its grease melts into the flames. Light washes over the rim of your sandal and catches two wasps decorating the hazy screened window.

My grandmother would have delighted in such an evening. The chimes stirred by the wind remind me of her tea trolley, its china rattling as she pushed it across the rocky yard on Cook Street during a summer when I could never quench my thirst. From my lawn chair, I watched her travel back and forth like a mechanical figure on a clock. She cleaned me with alcohol and trimmed my hair using a straight razor.

Only a week had passed since I left the hospital. Below my breasts, surgical thread held an incision closed. The surgeon’s blade had passed so near my heart that it seemed to brush it briefly, and I almost lost my life. Even after many years, I can picture the flesh trembling inside my left breast. My heart now moves unevenly, like a great-uncle who was both Jewish and disabled and was hauled across the steppes by Cossacks. In the end, he was like a companion pleading with a horse for help—a horse that ran with such flawless force that the green grass seemed to lift itself toward him.
outputs.L3:
In Tunis, the speaker’s attempts to confront the difficult subjects of divorce and death gradually give way to a quieter, more immediate experience: resting with rug merchants beneath a plum tree. The scene is filled with vivid, almost dreamlike images—a severed lamb’s head, flickering fire, hovering insects, and the soft light of evening. Together, these details create an atmosphere in which beauty and mortality are inseparable, as though ordinary life continues in intimate proximity to violence, decay, and loss.

As night falls, the speaker is drawn into memories of childhood and of a grandmother who cared for them while they recovered from surgery. The operation had nearly proved fatal, leaving both a visible scar and permanent damage to the heart. This injured heart becomes more than a physical organ; it serves as a symbol of vulnerability, survival, and inherited pain. The speaker compares it to a lame Jewish great-uncle fleeing cossacks on horseback. Through this striking comparison, private trauma becomes connected to ancestral persecution, suggesting that the speaker’s wounded heart carries not only the memory of personal suffering but also the historical suffering of earlier generations.
outputs.L4:
Set against the vivid sights and sensations of Tunis, the poem becomes a meditation on mortality, divorce, illness, and inherited trauma. The city’s streets, buildings, and atmosphere do more than establish a setting: they act as emotional triggers, carrying the speaker from the present into intimate memories of family, bodily suffering, and historical violence. Images encountered in Tunis evoke the speaker’s grandmother and the fragile continuity between generations, while recollections of surgery return the poem to the vulnerability of the body. The speaker’s near-death experience is not confined to the past; it remains active in the present, shaping how love, separation, and survival are understood.

The poem’s shifting imagery mirrors the movement of memory itself. Personal experiences blend with stories of Jewish persecution, suggesting that the speaker’s pain belongs both to an individual life and to a larger ancestral history. The wounded heart is therefore at once literal and symbolic: it is a body altered by illness and medical intervention, a self marked by divorce and emotional loss, and an inheritance burdened by collective suffering. Yet the poem does not present survival as simple recovery. To survive is to continue carrying scars, memories, and the knowledge of how close death can be.

By linking the speaker’s medical crisis to the endurance of earlier generations, the poem enlarges the meaning of resilience. The grandmother’s presence and the history of persecution become reminders that survival often involves preserving memory even when that memory is painful. Tunis serves as the place where these different times and experiences converge. Through its layered scenes and associative movement, the poem shows how the present is haunted—but also sustained—by the past. Ultimately, it portrays identity as something formed through bodily vulnerability, intimate loss, ancestral trauma, and the difficult, ongoing act of living.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem set in Tunis that intertwines travel, mortality, family memory, illness, and Jewish ancestry through vivid sensory imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
**Salt Line**

In Tunis, the morning opens blue shutters  
with a hand smelling of coffee and iron.

Along Avenue de France,  
taxis flare yellow as fever,  
and the tram’s bell scatters pigeons  
over the white shoulders of the cathedral.

I have come with one suitcase,  
my mother’s cough folded inside it,  
her hospital bracelet tucked  
between shirts like a boarding pass  
to a country none of us names.

At the market, oranges split under the knife—  
small suns, bleeding sweetness.  
Cumin, harissa, mint crushed underfoot;  
fish on beds of ice stare upward  
with the calm of the already departed.

I follow the streets toward the sea,  
past walls where salt lifts the paint  
in pale scales,  
past doorways blue as the evil-eye beads  
my grandmother pinned above our cradle.

She was born near here, she said,  
or perhaps the story was born here—  
in the Hara, among brass lamps,  
sewing needles, Sabbath bread,  
and women calling from balcony to balcony  
while the soup breathed coriander.

Her father sang Hebrew  
with a Tunisian ache in the vowels.  
Her mother lit two candles  
and covered her eyes  
as if darkness were another homeland  
one could enter by blessing.

Later came ships, papers,  
names bent at border desks,  
photographs where the dead remain young  
because silver does not understand illness.

At the synagogue, wax pools  
beneath the flames.  
I touch the cool wall,  
thinking of marrow, of blood counts,  
of my mother asleep beneath a white sheet  
while machines count what the body  
has forgotten to keep.

Outside, children kick a red ball  
against Roman stone.  
Each strike returns it to them.

What is ancestry  
but this stubborn rebound—  
a word crossing centuries,  
a recipe surviving in the mouth,  
the scent of orange blossom  
rising from a cake no one remembers  
how to make?

By evening, Carthage burns softly  
under the descending sun.  
The ruins hold their broken columns  
like old men holding canes.

I sit above the gulf  
and eat bread torn by hand,  
olives black and shining,  
salt bright on my lips.

Across the water, ferries move  
with their necklaces of light.

Somewhere, my mother wakes.  
Somewhere, my grandmother is still  
closing the shutters before dusk.  
Somewhere, the first star appears  
over Tunis,

and every journey becomes a return,  
every body a brief hotel  
where the ancestors unpack their names,  
leave the windows open,

and listen to the sea  
entering, leaving—  
entering, leaving—  
as if death were only breath  
traveling farther than we can follow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a surreal narrative poem in which a woman recovering from heart surgery remembers her grandmother and imagines a lame Jewish great-uncle fleeing Cossacks.
counterfactuals.output:
**After the Sternum Opens**

She wakes with a red seam  
stitched down her chest,  
a narrow railway the surgeons have left  
for the heart to travel home.

In the hospital window  
the moon wears a paper mask.  
Machines beside her bed  
breathe in blue syllables.  
Every few minutes her pulse  
knocks over a glass in another room.

She remembers her grandmother  
rolling dough beneath her palms,  
flour whitening the dark hairs  
on her arms—

*Not too thin,* Grandmother warned,  
though she may have meant the pastry,  
or winter,  
or the veil between the living  
and those who continue  
setting places at the table.

Morphine loosens the ceiling.

Through it comes a village  
upside down: chimneys rooted in clouds,  
geese floating like handkerchiefs,  
a well drawing buckets  
from the bottom of the sky.

And there—her great-uncle,  
the one no photograph kept,  
lame in one leg, running.

How can a lame man run?

With one foot on earth  
and one foot in the Book of Exodus.  
With his crutch under one arm  
and the Sabbath candlesticks under the other.  
With Cossack horses breaking  
the black bread of the road behind him.

He runs through a forest  
where every birch is a pale grandmother.  
They lift their branches and say,  
*Here, child. Here is another way.*

Snow enters his shoes.  
The moon rolls beside him  
like a silver wheel torn from a cart.  
He loses a button, a prayer,  
the name of a river.

But not the candlesticks.

Never the candlesticks.

In her hospital bed,  
the woman feels him stumble  
inside the newly opened chamber of her chest.  
She wants to call out,  
but her voice is still asleep  
under gauze.

So she sends him her heartbeat:

one knock for the border,  
two for the frozen field,  
three for the door  
that has not yet appeared.

Her grandmother opens it.

She is young now, younger  
than the woman has ever known her,  
her apron full of warm stars.  
She takes the uncle’s crutch,  
takes the candles,  
takes his ruined foot in both hands  
and washes it with milk.

The Cossacks ride past  
as a storm of empty coats.

Morning gathers at the window.  
A nurse enters carrying pills  
in a small paper cup.

The woman looks down  
at the scar’s red ladder  
and understands recovery  
as an old family art:

to flee without leaving,  
to carry fire through snow,  
to wake beneath a white sheet  
while the dead, in the next room,  
knead the stubborn dough of the world.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a lyrical poem that begins beneath a plum tree with rug merchants and a roasting lamb, then shifts into memories of childhood, hospitalization, and inherited trauma.
counterfactuals.output:
Beneath the plum tree, rug merchants unrolled  
their woven countries over the dust—  
pomegranates, antlers, indigo rivers—  
while a lamb turned slowly above the coals,  
its bright fat hissing into flame.  
Someone lifted a cup. Someone named the dead  
as casually as naming weather.  
Purple fruit fell soundlessly around us,  
bruising the white cloth with summer.

And suddenly I was seven again,  
kneeling in the orchard’s green chapel,  
my pockets full of stones and sour plums,  
my mother calling from the doorway  
with the voice she used before sorrow  
made a locked room of her throat.

Childhood returns in fragments:  
a red bicycle abandoned in rain,  
the mineral smell of the school stairwell,  
my father washing blood from his hands  
though no wound could be found,  
my grandmother folding and refolding  
a letter written in a language  
she forbade herself to speak.

Then the hospital—  
its corridors polished to a moonlit pallor,  
its clocks chewing the same hour.  
A needle entered my arm  
like a thin question.  
Machines kept watch in blue numerals.  
Behind the curtain, someone prayed;  
behind my eyelids, the plum tree  
shook its dark bells into the grass.

All night the old griefs gathered:  
the train my grandfather would not describe,  
the cellar where the women learned silence,  
the border stitched through the family  
like black thread through a wedding cloth.  
What they buried became our weather.  
What they swallowed flowered in our sleep.  
We inherited not the story  
but the flinch before its telling.

Morning came carrying broth, clean bandages,  
the soft bureaucracy of survival.  
I thought of the merchants rolling their rugs,  
how every pattern hid a road,  
how every road curled toward a vanished house.  
I thought of the lamb’s small bones  
whitening beside the fire.

Above us, plums were ripening—  
each one holding a dusk-colored sweetness,  
each one carrying, inside its flesh,  
the hard stone of what came before.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an intimate, image-rich poem about nearly dying, using fragmented recollections, unexpected metaphors, and transitions between North Africa, a grandmother’s yard, and the Russian steppes.
counterfactuals.output:
I remember the light first—  
North Africa, noon,  
white as a bone held to the sun.

Then the road loosening beneath us,  
the car turning once, twice,  
a coin refusing to choose a face.

Someone called my name  
from very far away,  
or from inside my blood.

*

My grandmother’s yard:  
apricots bruising the grass,  
ants stitching their black grammar  
through spilled sugar.

She bent over the washbasin,  
wringing a sheet  
as if twisting rain from a cloud.

Don’t sleep, she said—  
though she had been dead nine years,  
though sand filled my mouth  
with its small, golden teeth.

*

There are moments the body becomes  
a house under renovation:  
doors removed,  
walls opened to weather,  
strangers walking through  
with buckets of red light.

I saw my hands  
floating above me—  
two pale fish  
that had forgotten water.

I saw the sky  
button and unbutton itself.

*

Then: the Russian steppes.

No road.  
Only grass leaning east  
under an iron wind,  
horses dark as burnt bread  
moving along the horizon.

I was there without a coat,  
without language,  
carrying my grandmother’s blue bowl  
against my chest.

Snow entered it silently.

Snow, or morphine.  
Snow, or the voices of nurses  
folding the night into quarters.

*

Fragments:

a siren swallowing distance—

the smell of diesel—

my mother’s wedding ring  
cold against my forehead—

a fly circling the ceiling  
like a black planet—

someone saying stay  
as if stay were a country,  
as if I had papers.

*

I nearly left.

Not upward—  
no ladder of angels,  
no radiant gate—

but sideways,

into the apricot shade,  
into the long grass,  
into that noon where the dunes  
were sleeping lions  
and every grain of sand  
kept one syllable of my name.

My grandmother stood by the fence  
in her flowered dress.

Behind her, Russia opened  
mile after mile,  
a green silence combed by wind.

Behind that, the desert burned  
without consuming itself.

She did not beckon.

She only lifted the blue bowl  
and poured the snow onto the roots  
of a young fig tree.

*

When I woke,  
the world was embarrassingly alive:

tape pulling at my skin,  
a machine blinking green,  
someone’s coffee cooling nearby.

My heart—  
that stubborn, wet match—  
struck again.

And somewhere, I swear,  
horses broke into a run.

Apricots fell softly in the yard.

Across North Africa  
the sun dragged its bright knife  
over the earth

and spared me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a contemporary free-verse meditation on divorce and death that includes Tunisian street life, wind chimes, surgical scars, a damaged heart, and an ancestral escape on horseback.
counterfactuals.output:
After the papers were signed,  
Tunis kept moving—

scooters threading the avenue,  
coffee spoons striking glass,  
a fishmonger lifting silver bodies  
into the blue argument of morning.

Nothing paused for our divorce.  
Not the boy selling jasmine,  
not the old men beneath the awning  
rearranging history over cigarettes,  
not the cat asleep beside the butcher’s door.

At night, wind chimes worried the balcony,  
small metal tongues translating the sea.  
You said the sound was peaceful.  
I heard cutlery in an empty house.

Death had already taught us  
how absence enters:  
not as thunder,  
but as a chair no one moves,  
a number still saved in the phone,  
surgical scars whitening  
across the body’s stubborn country.

The doctor called my heart damaged.  
I imagined it dented like a taxi  
that had survived too many roundabouts,  
still carrying strangers,  
still stopping when someone raised a hand.

My grandmother once escaped on horseback—  
or so the family tells it—  
her veil torn by acacia branches,  
the night opening and closing behind her,  
hoofbeats stitching distance  
between her life and the life chosen for her.

Perhaps that is what leaving is:  
not freedom, exactly,  
but wind against a wound,  
the knowledge that survival  
also leaves a scar.

Now the chimes speak whenever they please.  
Down in the street, vendors call,  
plates break, engines flare,  
someone laughs with their whole unbroken body.

I stand at the window  
with my ruined inheritance—  
the dead, the divorced,  
the horse still running in my blood—

and let the city pass through me,  
bright and indifferent,  
carrying everything away  
except the sound  
of having lived.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
